stem: A client has an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) result and assumes this confirms prostate cancer. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: An elevated PSA is not diagnostic by itself; prostate cancer can raise PSA, but benign enlargement, inflammation, and other factors can also increase it.
options.B: An elevated PSA confirms prostate cancer by itself because benign prostate conditions and recent prostate inflammation do not meaningfully affect the result.
options.C: An elevated PSA has no established clinical relevance because prostate cells do not normally produce PSA and cancer does not alter serum concentrations.
options.D: An elevated PSA is considered normal in every man over age 50 regardless of the actual value, symptoms, examination, medications, or prior results.

rationale: NCI states that PSA is produced by normal as well as malignant prostate cells and that both prostate cancer and benign conditions such as BPH and prostatitis can increase blood PSA. NCI also notes there is no single PSA level that by itself means a person has prostate cancer. Therefore A is correct; B overstates specificity, C is false, and D applies an unsupported blanket age rule.
educational_objective: Explain that an elevated PSA is a nonspecific finding that requires clinical interpretation rather than serving as a stand-alone diagnosis of prostate cancer.
source_locator: What is the PSA test?; What is a normal PSA test result? — PSA from normal/malignant cells; BPH/prostatitis can elevate PSA; no specific PSA level diagnoses cancer.
source_claim_supported: Elevated PSA is not diagnostic of prostate cancer because benign prostate conditions and other factors can also elevate PSA.

source_original.stem: A client has an elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) result and assumes this confirms prostate cancer. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: An elevated PSA is not diagnostic by itself; prostate cancer can raise PSA, but benign enlargement, inflammation, and other factors can also increase it.
options.B: An elevated PSA confirms prostate cancer by itself because benign prostate conditions and recent prostate inflammation do not meaningfully affect the result.
options.C: An elevated PSA has no established clinical relevance because prostate cells do not normally produce PSA and cancer does not alter serum concentrations.
options.D: An elevated PSA is considered normal in every man over age 50 regardless of the actual value, symptoms, examination, medications, or prior results.

source_original.rationale: PSA is produced by normal and malignant prostate cells, and elevated values can occur with prostate cancer as well as benign conditions such as BPH and prostatitis. Option A is correct because an elevated PSA requires clinical interpretation and possible further evaluation rather than serving as a stand-alone diagnosis. Option B overstates specificity. Option C is false. Option D incorrectly applies an age-based blanket rule.
source_original.source_detail: National Cancer Institute — Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) Test Fact Sheet: PSA is produced by normal and malignant prostate cells; levels can rise with prostate cancer but also with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis/inflammation, and other factors, so an elevated PSA alone does not diagnose prostate cancer. Current NCI PSA Fact Sheet live-rechecked 2026-08-15; difficulty corrected to easy because the item tests direct interpretation of a nonspecific tumor marker rather than multistep clinical judgment. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic probability tools, laboratory/tumor-marker interpretation, ECG/lab monitoring and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained original construct/key after current NCI verification; avoided introducing a universal PSA cutoff because NCI states no single level diagnoses cancer.

audit_findings.claim_audit: No universal diagnostic cutoff is asserted.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A is consistent with NCI guidance.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are interpretations of elevated PSA.
